notes.meaning: After traveling from Babylon and settling into their towns, the Jewish people gathered together in Jerusalem as one body. The seventh month in early autumn was the most sacred season of their year, filled with major feasts. Even though they were busy building their own homes, they chose to put worship first and assembled with one heart to seek God.

Jeshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the civil governor led the priests and people in rebuilding the altar of God. An altar was a stone table where animal offerings were made to seek God's forgiveness and give Him thanks. They took care to build it and sacrifice on it strictly according to the Law of Moses. They knew they needed God's blessing and forgiveness before they could start rebuilding the temple itself.

The leaders set the altar on its ancient foundation amid the ruins of the city. The people felt deep fear because of the hostile groups living in the surrounding lands, which drove them to seek God's help at once. By restarting the required morning and evening burnt offerings every day, they placed their safety in the hands of the Lord.

The returned exiles celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles by living in temporary leafy shelters, just as the Law of Moses commanded. This week-long festival reminded them of how God watched over their ancestors during forty years in the desert after leaving Egypt. Having just finished their own long trek from Babylon, the feast had special meaning, and they offered every sacrifice required for each day.

Once the festival ended, the priests continued the regular schedule of morning and evening sacrifices. They also presented the offerings commanded for the start of each month and for all the annual sacred feasts, as well as voluntary gifts that individuals brought from willing hearts. Their generosity showed great devotion to the Lord, even though they had very little wealth.

The priests began offering burnt sacrifices on the very first day of the seventh month, even though not a single stone of the temple foundation had yet been laid. They did not wait for a grand building to be completed before honoring God. Setting up the altar first showed that a restored relationship with the Lord was far more important than the building itself.

The Jewish leaders paid money to masons and carpenters, and gave wheat, wine, and olive oil to the Phoenician traders of Tyre and Sidon. In return, the Phoenicians floated large cedar logs down the Mediterranean coast from Lebanon to the port of Joppa, just as Solomon had arranged centuries earlier. King Cyrus of Persia had officially given them permission to gather these building supplies.

Construction on the temple began in the second month of their second year in Jerusalem, which was mid-spring when the dry season kept the ground firm. Zerubbabel, Jeshua, the priests, and all the returned exiles united to start the work. They appointed Levites who were twenty years old or older to oversee the construction, following the pattern King David had established.

Jeshua the Levite and his family, along with Kadmiel and the sons of Henadad, stepped forward to supervise the builders. These Levitical family heads worked together with single-minded unity to direct and encourage the laborers. Their close cooperation helped ensure that the construction on God's house moved forward smoothly and in good order.

When the builders finished laying the foundation of the temple, the leaders held a formal service of praise. The priests stood in their special sacred clothing blowing trumpets, while the Levites from the family of Asaph played bronze cymbals. They followed the exact instructions for temple music that King David had given long before.

The choirs sang back and forth in turns, praising God and thanking Him because He is good and His faithful love to Israel endures forever. As soon as the foundation was laid, the entire assembly raised a thunderous shout of praise. Even when God's work is only beginning, His people have good reason to rejoice with thankful hearts.

While many people shouted with joy, many elderly priests, Levites, and family leaders wept loudly when they saw the foundation. These older men were old enough to remember Solomon's magnificent temple before it was burned fifty years earlier, and they saw how small and humble this new building would be. At the same time, the younger generation shouted with pure joy because they had never seen a temple in Jerusalem before.

The shouts of joy and the sounds of loud weeping blended together into one massive roar. The noise was so loud and mixed that no one could tell the cries of grief from the cheers of praise, and the sound carried far into the distance. This scene shows that deep sorrow over past loss and genuine joy over new beginnings often exist side by side among God's people.
